User: I need help with my 2023 tax return. I'm head of household in Chicago IL. My W-2 from TechStart Inc shows $64,800. I had $15,000 in 1099 income (marketing, 2 clients), $1,450 from Goldman Sachs Marcus, and $320 from TD Ameritrade. I have a home office (140 sq ft, exclusive use); rent is $2,400/month for 620 sq ft total. Student loan interest: $3,600 (Navient, 2017–2019). I donated $1,350 to St. Mary's Food Bank (have the receipt) have receipt, and had $1,350 in work expenses. What can I deduct, and should I itemize or take the standard deduction? What forms do I need?
Assistant: Thanks — this has enough detail to give a clear picture. Below I’ll (1) list what deductions you can claim, (2) estimate whether itemizing makes sense, (3) list the IRS/state forms you’ll need, and (4) ask two quick clarifying questions that could change the results.

Important quick note: I’m not your tax preparer — this is a general explanation based on the amounts you gave. For final filing or complex questions, consider a CPA or tax preparer.

1) What you can (likely) deduct
- W-2 wages (TechStart Inc): report as wage income on Form 1040 (W-2).
- 1099 freelance income ($15,000): report on Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business). From Schedule C you can deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses related to that 1099 work (see below).
  - Business expenses: the $1,350 you listed — if those were expenses of your marketing business (supplies, software, client expenses, marketing, etc.) they are deductible on Schedule C. If they were unreimbursed employee expenses related to your W-2 job, those are NOT deductible for 2018–2025 on your federal return.
  - Home office: Because you have an exclusive-use home office (140 sq ft of a 620 sq ft apartment), you can take a home-office deduction for the self-employed/ Schedule C business. Two methods:
    - Simplified: $5/sq ft × 140 = $700.
    - Actual/regular method: business percentage = 140/620 ≈ 22.58% of home expenses. For rent of $2,400/mo ($28,800/yr), the home-office share of rent ≈ $6,506. (If you have utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., you’d apportion the business share of those too — increasing the deduction.)
    - To use the actual method you’ll calculate and report via Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) with Schedule C.
  - Self-employment tax: you’ll owe SE tax on net self-employment income and can deduct half of the SE tax as an adjustment to income on Form 1040.
  - Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: if you have net qualified business income from your Schedule C, you’ll likely be eligible for the 20% QBI deduction (Form 8995) because your income is well below the phase-out thresholds.
- Interest income ($1,450 from Goldman Sachs Marcus + $320 from TD Ameritrade = $1,770): taxable interest reported on Form 1040. Because taxable interest > $1,500, you’ll need Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends).
- Student loan interest ($3,600): the maximum student loan interest deduction for 2023 is $2,500 and it is an above-the-line deduction (reported on Schedule 1). However:
  - It only applies to interest you actually paid in the tax year (2023). If the $3,600 is interest paid in 2023, you can only deduct up to $2,500 (subject to MAGI phase-out). If the $3,600 refers to interest accrued or paid in earlier years (2017–2019), that cannot be deducted on the 2023 return.
  - Phaseout: the deduction phases out for single/head-of-household filers with MAGI between $75,000 and $90,000 (for 2023). If your MAGI is under $75k you can take the full (up to $2,500); over $90k you cannot take it. (I estimate your MAGI is likely under that threshold — see the estimates below.)
- Charitable donation ($1,350 to St. Mary’s): deductible only if you itemize on Schedule A. (No special above-the-line deduction applies for 2023 cash gifts.)
- State & local taxes (SALT): you can deduct state income tax and/or property taxes on Schedule A, but the SALT deduction is capped at $10,000. You didn’t list state income tax or property tax paid — include those if you have them.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses for W-2: Not deductible on federal (suspended through 2025).

2) Itemize vs standard deduction — likely result
- Standard deduction for Head of Household (2023): $20,800.
- Your listed itemizable amounts on Schedule A, as stated: charitable $1,350. Unless you have substantial state income/property taxes, mortgage interest, or other itemized items that bring Schedule A above $20,800, you should take the standard deduction.
- Note: the home office deduction and business expenses do NOT affect the decision to itemize — those are business deductions on Schedule C and reduce your AGI regardless. So even if you take the standard deduction for personal items, you still can (and should) claim your business and home-office deductions.

3) Forms you will likely need
Federal
- Form 1040 (individual income tax return).
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments) — for the student loan interest deduction (and any other adjustments).
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report the $15,000 1099 income and business expenses.
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you use the actual-method home-office deduction. If you use the simplified method ($5/sq ft), you can report the deduction on Schedule C without Form 8829.
- Schedule SE — to compute self-employment tax for the 1099 income.
- Form 8995 (or 8995-A if required) — for the QBI (20%) deduction. Most taxpayers with income below the threshold use Form 8995.
- Schedule B — because your taxable interest ($1,770) exceeds $1,500.
- Schedule A — only if you choose to itemize (seems unlikely based on the numbers you gave).
State (Illinois)
- IL-1040 — Illinois state return. (Illinois has a flat income tax; you still must report federal adjustments per IL rules; any state-specific credits or forms depend on your situation.)

4) Rough estimate (with assumptions)
Assumptions used: the $1,350 work expenses are legitimate business expenses for the 1099 work; the $3,600 student loan interest was paid in 2023 (see clarifying Q below), and you use the actual home-office method with no other home expenses included except rent.

Quick calculation (approximate):
- W-2 wages: $64,800
- 1099 gross: $15,000
- Interest income: $1,770
Gross income ≈ $81,570

Schedule C deductions (approx):
- Home office (actual): 22.58% × $28,800 rent ≈ $6,506
- Other business expenses: $1,350
Net self-employment income ≈ $15,000 − $7,856 ≈ $7,144

Self-employment tax ≈ $1,009 → half deductible ≈ $504

AGI estimate ≈ wages (64,800) + net SE (7,144) + interest (1,770) − half SE tax (504) ≈ $73,210

Student loan interest deduction: up to $2,500 (if eligible) → AGI after student loan interest ≈ $70,710

Standard deduction (HOH) = $20,800 → estimated taxable income ≈ $49,910 (before QBI)

QBI deduction: ~20% of QBI ≈ 0.20 × $7,144 ≈ $1,429 → taxable income reduced to ≈ $48,480.

Takeaway from this estimate:
- You’ll still be well under the standard deduction, so itemizing almost certainly doesn’t help unless you have significant state/property taxes or large other itemizable expenses.
- The home-office deduction and other business expenses materially reduce your taxable income and self-employment tax base; be sure to claim them correctly on Schedule C (and Form 8829 if using actual method).
- Student loan interest will likely be limited to $2,500 (not the full $3,600), and is subject to the MAGI phaseout (you’re likely under the $75k limit under these assumptions).
- Expect to owe (or have additional) self-employment tax because of the 1099 income (Schedule SE), although net SE income is relatively modest once home-office and business expenses are included.

5) Quick clarifying questions
I need two clarifications because they materially affect the numbers:
1. Are the $1,350 in "work expenses" business expenses related to your 1099 marketing work (i.e., deductible on Schedule C), or are they unreimbursed employee expenses from your W-2 job? (If they’re W-2 unreimbursed expenses, they are not deductible federally for 2018–2025.)
2. Did you actually pay $3,600 of student loan interest in calendar year 2023 (and receive a 1098-E for 2023)? Or does $3,600 refer to interest paid in earlier years (2017–2019)? Only interest actually paid in 2023 is deductible on the 2023 return.

6) Next steps I can help with
- If you confirm answers to the two questions above, I can run a more precise calculation of taxable income, expected federal income tax, and self-employment tax (estimate).
- I can also draft a checklist of documents to gather for your preparer (W-2, 1099s, 1098-E, receipts, rent/utility bills for home-office proof, etc.).
- Or if you’d like, I can prepare a draft email to your tax preparer listing these numbers and asking for filing help.

Tell me the answers to the two clarifying questions and what you’d like next (estimate, checklist, or email to preparer).
